Each row is a township, grouped by front, and each column is a quarter; a red cell means the township was a hot spot that quarter, a blue cell a cold spot, and the dashed line marks late 2023, when Operation 1027 began and fighting resumed in Rakhine. Not one war but several: in the Dry Zone, eleven townships have been hot every quarter since late 2021, and the zone has grown, reaching Pyinoolwin in 2024 and Nyaung-U and Chauk in 2025. Most of northern Shan was hot for only two quarters around Operation 1027, and only its western edge stayed hot. Rakhine was mostly cold until 2024, hot through 2024 and into early 2025, and by late 2025 only Kyaukpyu was still hot. On the Thai border and in Bago, several townships have been hot almost without a break for about three years, and Kayah and Chin were hot early in the war and have since faded. Hot status is measured against the rest of the country each quarter, so a township can drop out because fighting grew elsewhere, as in Chin, rather than because it became calmer; the raw counts below show that the decline in Kayah, by contrast, is real.

### Dry Zone: a sustained core that has spread

**Evidence.** `r sum(ehsa$class == "Consecutive hot spot")` townships are consecutive hot spots. Eleven, in lower Sagaing, northern Magway and Mandalay, have been hot in every quarter since Q3 or Q4 2021: in substance persistent hot spots dating from the uprising, mostly without a significant trend. The zone has spread: Madaya joined in Q4 2022, Mogoke (sporadic) in Q4 2023, Pyinoolwin in Q3 2024, and Nyaung-U and Chauk, down the Ayeyarwady, in Q1 2025, each staying hot with a significant upward trend. This explains Pyinoolwin's LISA Low-High status (@sec-lmsa): quiet until mid-2024, hot every quarter since. Monywa, the highest total nationally, was hot for 15 consecutive quarters but not the last, so it is sporadic.

**Context.** The core matches the People's Defence Force uprising in the Bamar heartland [@iiss2022dryzone]. The spread towards Mandalay matches the second phase of Operation 1027 from June 2024, when the TNLA took Mogoke, Mandalay PDFs fought in Madaya, Singu and Thabeikkyin, and Brotherhood forces threatened Pyinoolwin [@iiss2024mandalay; @rfa2024pyinoolwin]. We found no source for the 2025 spread to Nyaung-U and Chauk; it should be checked before being relied on.

### Northern Shan: intense but short-lived

**Evidence.** Laukkaing, Kunlong, Hopang, Hseni, Kutkai, Muse and Namhkan were all hot in Q4 2023 and Q1 2024 and never since; Lashio was hot once more, in Q4 2024. By mid-2025, Laukkaing, Kunlong, Hopang, Kutkai, Lashio and Manton were significant *cold* spots (oscillating cold), and Kutkai, Muse and Namhkan trend downwards. Two hot quarters of 19 are too few to register in a 57-month total, which answers the LMSA's open question: northern Shan was a hot spot, briefly. The western edge differs: Nawnghkio has been hot every quarter since Q2 2023, trending upwards, and Kyaukme since Q1 2024.

**Context.** The hot quarters span Operation 1027 (27 October 2023) and the China-brokered ceasefire of 12 January 2024 [@iiss2023op1027]. Lashio's hot quarter follows its capture by the MNDAA in August 2024; the MNDAA handed it back in April 2025 under Chinese pressure [@irrawaddy2025lashio], just before the cold quarters. In the west, fighting moved towards Mandalay and then reversed, with the military retaking Nawnghkio in July 2025 [@myanmarnow2025nawnghkio]. A holding ceasefire is a plausible reading of the 2025 cold spots, but the data show only that few events were reported.

### Rakhine: cold, then hot, then quiet

**Evidence.** `r sum(ehsa$ST == "Rakhine" & ehsa$class == "No pattern detected")` of Rakhine's 17 townships are "no pattern detected", a label that hides a clear sequence. Most were repeatedly *cold* in 2021–2023, apart from one hot quarter in the north in Q4 2022. They turned hot from Q1 2024 in the north and centre, and between Q3 2024 and Q1 2025 in the south (Toungup, Thandwe, Gwa). By Q3 2025 only Kyaukpyu, hot from Q1 to Q3 2025, remained hot; it is an oscillating hot spot. `sfdep` has no category for "cold, then hot, then neither", so the rest fall to "no pattern". Sittwe is a sporadic cold spot.

**Context.** This follows the Arakan Army's campaign. An informal ceasefire held from late 2020 apart from clashes in 2022; the offensive began on 13 November 2023, and by end-December 2024 the AA held 14 of 17 townships, including Maungdaw, Toungup, Gwa and the Western Command at Ann [@diplomat2024ann]. The military kept Sittwe, Kyaukpyu and Munaung, and the AA attacked Kyaukpyu from February 2025 [@rfa2025kyaukpyu]. The 2025 quiet fits consolidated AA control, with fighting shifting to the remaining enclaves and neighbouring regions [@stimson2025arakan]. "No pattern" here does not mean no conflict.

### South-east: Bago, Kayin and Tanintharyi

**Evidence.** In Bago (East), Kyauktaga was cold for four quarters in 2021–2022 and Htantabin for one; both have been hot in most quarters since mid-2023 and trend upwards (oscillating hot). Phyu followed the same path but was not significant in the final quarter ("no pattern"). Shwegyin has been hot every quarter since Q3 2022, and Kyaukkyi in all but one since Q1 2023. On the Thai border, Hlaingbwe was hot in 16 of 19 quarters and Myawaddy in 13, with a gap in late 2024. Dawei and Palaw (Tanintharyi) have been hot every quarter since mid-2022. "Sporadic" here (Shwegyin, Kyaukkyi, Kayin) means hot almost always with one or two gaps, not occasional flare-ups. The LMSA called these hot spots fragile because they fail FDR (@sec-lmsa-robust); three years of significant quarters strengthen the case that they are real.

**Context.** The Bago pattern matches a new front along the old Yangon–Mandalay road, where Bago PDFs and KNU Brigade 3 escalated attacks in early 2025 [@irrawaddy2025bago]. The Kayin hot spot includes the fight for Myawaddy in April 2024 [@csis2024myawaddy].

### Karenni and Chin: early fronts that lost prominence

**Evidence.** Demoso, Hpruso and Pekon were hot every quarter from mid-2021 to Q3 2023 and never afterwards; Loikaw, Hakha, Falam and Mindat follow the same shape with gaps. All are sporadic hot spots, and Demoso, Hakha and Mindat trend downwards. Because Gi\* is relative, raw counts are needed to tell a real decline from being overtaken. In Kayah, events fell from about 110 a quarter in 2021–2023 to about 40 in 2024–2025: a real decline. In Chin, counts stayed near 100 a quarter until end-2024, so its loss of status from late 2023 is mainly relative, as new fronts in northern Shan, Rakhine and Mandalay overtook it.

### Cold spots: ceasefire zones, the delta and Yangon

**Evidence.** The `r sum(ehsa$class == "Persistent cold spot")` persistent cold spots are significant in at least 18 of 19 quarters: 15 in the Wa and eastern and southern Shan hills, 6 in the delta and Poke Ba Thi Ri in Nay Pyi Taw. Yangon differs: `r sum(ehsa$ST == "Yangon" & ehsa$class == "Consecutive cold spot")` of its 44 townships are *consecutive* cold spots, `r sum(ehsa$ST == "Yangon" & ehsa$class == "Consecutive cold spot" & ehsa$cold_run_start %in% 8:10)` of them with cold runs starting between Q4 2022 and Q2 2023. Few were cold before 2022. Yangon's events fell from 240–330 a quarter in Q2–Q4 2021 to about 40–80 from 2023.

**Context.** Yangon's early conflict was dominated by the post-coup crackdown [@cfr_myanmar]; the data show armed conflict then moved away, not why. Firmer military control and the Wa ceasefire are plausible explanations for the cold spots [@aljazeera2024sacm], beyond what the statistic can show.

## Sensitivity of the EHSA classes {#sec-ehsa-sens}

```{r}
#| label: ehsa-sens
fit_q_seed <- ehsa_gi(X_q, nb_ehsa, seed = 2026)
fit_q_knn  <- ehsa_gi(X_q, nb_knn6_ehsa)

ehsa_sens <- tibble(
  primary  = ehsa$class,
  thr_025  = pretty_class(classify_ehsa(fit_q$gi, fit_q$p, 0.025)$classification),
  thr_01   = pretty_class(classify_ehsa(fit_q$gi, fit_q$p, 0.01)$classification),
  seed2026 = pretty_class(classify_ehsa(fit_q_seed$gi, fit_q_seed$p, 0.05)$classification),
  knn6     = pretty_class(classify_ehsa(fit_q_knn$gi, fit_q_knn$p, 0.05)$classification),
  monthly  = pretty_class(m_fixed$classification))

core_consecutive <- ehsa$class == "Consecutive hot spot"

sens_spec <- c(thr_025 = "Threshold 0.025", thr_01 = "Threshold 0.01 (sfdep default)",
               seed2026 = "Different seed (2026)", knn6 = "KNN k = 6 neighbours",
               monthly = "Monthly cube (57 slices)")
imap_dfr(sens_spec, function(label, col) {
  alt <- ehsa_sens[[col]]
  tibble(specification = label,
         same_class  = paste0(round(100 * mean(alt == ehsa_sens$primary)), "%"),
         same_family = paste0(round(100 * mean(family_of(alt) == ehsa$family)), "%"),
         hot_cold_flips = sum(family_of(alt) != "None" & ehsa$family != "None" &
                                family_of(alt) != ehsa$family),
         consecutive_hot_still_hot = paste0(sum(family_of(alt)[core_consecutive] == "Hot"),
                                            " of ", sum(core_consecutive)))
}) |>
  kable()

# Quarter in which each township is first a significant hot spot
first_hot_q <- function(fit, threshold) {
  apply(fit$p <= threshold & fit$gi > 0, 1, \(r) if (any(r)) which(r)[1] else NA)
}
is_hot   <- ehsa$family == "Hot"
shift_25 <- abs(first_hot_q(fit_q, 0.05) - first_hot_q(fit_q, 0.025))[is_hot]

ehsa_sens <- ehsa_sens |>
  mutate(n_hot  = rowSums(across(primary:monthly, \(x) family_of(x) == "Hot")),
         n_cold = rowSums(across(primary:monthly, \(x) family_of(x) == "Cold")))
```

**What the sensitivity checks show.**

- **The exact label is fragile.** Only `r ehsa_sens |> summarise(mean(thr_025 == primary)) |> pull() |> scales::percent()` of townships keep their class at threshold 0.025, and `r ehsa_sens |> summarise(mean(monthly == primary)) |> pull() |> scales::percent()` on the monthly cube, mostly switching between *consecutive* and *sporadic*, which both depend on unbroken runs. The Dry Zone core sits on the 90% boundary: with another seed, Yinmarbin reaches 18 hot quarters and becomes *diminishing*.
- **Hot or cold is robust.** 78% to 96% of townships keep their family under every alternative. Hot-to-cold flips are rare except under KNN, mostly townships with few hot quarters on the margins of fronts (Muse and Konkyan on the Chinese border, Tamu and Homalin on the Indian border) or around Mandalay city, where KNN reaches beyond shared borders. At least 15 of the 17 consecutive hot spots stay hot under each alternative, and Myaing, Yesagyo, Pakokku and Singu are consecutive under every one.
- **Timing is fairly robust.** At 0.025, `r sum(shift_25 <= 1, na.rm = TRUE)` of the `r sum(is_hot)` hot spot townships first turn hot in the same quarter as the primary run or one later; `r sum(is.na(shift_25))` have no hot quarter at the stricter threshold.

The categories are best read as shorthand for the timelines in @fig-ehsa-timeline. `r sum(ehsa_sens$n_hot == 6)` townships are hot and `r sum(ehsa_sens$n_cold == 6)` cold under all six runs; these are the EHSA results the integrated findings use.

# Integrated findings and discussion {#sec-integrated}

LMSA describes the *whole period*, EHSA *each quarter* and how they connect, and the bivariate analysis relates *two kinds* of violence. This section combines them and states how far each conclusion can be trusted.

## How the whole-period and quarterly views fit together

```{r}
#| label: integrated
integ <- ehsa |>
  select(TS_PCODE, ST, TS, conflict_n, class, family, hot_q, cold_q) |>
  mutate(n_hot6 = ehsa_sens$n_hot, n_cold6 = ehsa_sens$n_cold) |>   # same row order as ehsa
  left_join(select(hcsa, TS_PCODE, hcsa_class), by = "TS_PCODE") |>
  left_join(st_drop_geometry(mmr_an) |> select(TS_PCODE, pop2014), by = "TS_PCODE") |>
  mutate(gi = case_when(str_detect(hcsa_class, "^Hot")  ~ "Hot spot",
                        str_detect(hcsa_class, "^Cold") ~ "Cold spot",
                        TRUE                            ~ "Not significant"),
         evidence = case_when(
           n_hot6  == 6 & gi == "Hot spot"  ~ "Hot in the total and in all six EHSA runs",
           n_hot6  == 6                     ~ "Hot in all six EHSA runs only",
           n_cold6 == 6 & gi == "Cold spot" ~ "Cold in the total and in all six EHSA runs",
           n_cold6 == 6                     ~ "Cold in all six EHSA runs only",
           TRUE                             ~ "Other"))

# Whole-period Gi* against the quarterly EHSA family
table(`Gi* over the whole period` = integ$gi,
      `EHSA family (by quarter)`  = integ$family) |> kable()

# Strength of evidence: how many townships, how much of the conflict, how many people
integ |>
  group_by(evidence) |>
  summarise(townships = n(),
            share_of_events = scales::percent(sum(conflict_n) / sum(integ$conflict_n), accuracy = 1),
            census_2014_pop_m = round(sum(pop2014, na.rm = TRUE) / 1e6, 1)) |>
  arrange(match(evidence, c("Hot in the total and in all six EHSA runs", "Hot in all six EHSA runs only",
                            "Cold in the total and in all six EHSA runs", "Cold in all six EHSA runs only", "Other"))) |>
  kable()
```

The views never contradict each other: no township is a Gi\* hot spot and an EHSA cold spot, or the reverse. They differ in what they *see*. Of `r sum(integ$gi == "Hot spot")` whole-period hot spots, `r sum(integ$gi == "Hot spot" & integ$family == "Hot")` are hot-family in EHSA, and EHSA finds `r sum(integ$gi == "Not significant" & integ$family == "Hot")` more whose hot quarters were too few or scattered to lift the 57-month sum. Likewise for cold spots: `r sum(integ$gi == "Cold spot")` in the total, `r sum(integ$gi == "Not significant" & integ$family == "Cold")` more in EHSA.

```{r}
#| label: fig-map-integrated
#| fig-cap: "Where the three analyses agree. Dark colours are townships that are significant in the whole-period Gi* (p < 0.05) and in all six EHSA runs (primary, thresholds 0.025 and 0.01, a different seed, KNN neighbours and the monthly cube). Light colours are significant in all six EHSA runs but not in the whole-period Gi*. All other townships are grey."
#| fig-height: 9
#| fig-width: 9
ev_levels <- c("Hot in the total and in all six EHSA runs", "Hot in all six EHSA runs only",
                "Cold in the total and in all six EHSA runs", "Cold in all six EHSA runs only",
                "Other", "Not analysed")
ev_pal <- c("#67001f", "#f4a582", "#053061", "#92c5de", "#eeeeee", "#ffffff") |> setNames(ev_levels)

integ_map <- mmr_conflict |>
  select(TS_PCODE) |>
  left_join(select(integ, TS_PCODE, evidence), by = "TS_PCODE") |>
  mutate(evidence = factor(replace_na(evidence, "Not analysed"), levels = ev_levels))

tm_shape(integ_map) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "evidence",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(
                values = ev_pal,
                labels = c("Hot: total and all EHSA runs", "Hot: all EHSA runs only",
                           "Cold: total and all EHSA runs", "Cold: all EHSA runs only",
                           "Other", "Not analysed")),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Evidence",
                                      position = tm_pos_out("right", "center")),
              col = "grey60", lwd = 0.2) +
  map_furniture() +
  tm_compass(type = "arrow", size = 2.5,
             position = tm_pos_in("right", "top")) +
  tm_scalebar(breaks = c(0, 100, 200), text.size = 0.6,
              position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom"))
```

This map combines the hot spot test on the overall total with all six versions of the quarter-by-quarter analysis. Dark red townships are hot in both, light red townships are hot in every quarterly version but not in the overall total, the blues are the cold equivalents, and grey means the evidence is less consistent. The dark red core is mainly the Dry Zone belt, where both views agree conflict has been heavy and lasting (`r sum(integ$evidence == "Hot in the total and in all six EHSA runs")` townships). The light red townships (`r sum(integ$evidence == "Hot in all six EHSA runs only")`) are fronts that totals dilute, `r sum(integ$evidence == "Hot in all six EHSA runs only" & integ$ST %in% c("Kachin", "Shan (North)", "Chin", "Kayah", "Kayin", "Mon"))` of them in Kachin, northern Shan, Chin, Kayah, Kayin and Mon. Dark blue marks the Shan hills, the delta, Nay Pyi Taw and part of Yangon, low in the total too. Light blue is mostly Yangon (`r sum(integ$evidence == "Cold in all six EHSA runs only" & integ$ST == "Yangon")` townships), the delta, western Bago and southern Magway, where only the quarterly test finds sustained cold spots. The `r sum(integ$evidence %in% c("Hot in the total and in all six EHSA runs", "Hot in all six EHSA runs only"))` townships hot in all six EHSA runs hold `r scales::percent(sum(integ$conflict_n[integ$evidence %in% c("Hot in the total and in all six EHSA runs", "Hot in all six EHSA runs only")]) / sum(integ$conflict_n), accuracy = 1)` of all events; no township is hot in one method and cold in another. The map counts events, not people displaced today: about 3.6 million people were internally displaced in 2025, so the 2014 census figures behind the population estimate above are only a rough guide, and the map is a starting list for where protection and aid planning could focus, not a ranking of need.

## What the analyses say about each objective

**O1: where are the hot spots, cold spots and outliers?**

- **Hot spots.** One large Dry Zone concentration (Sagaing, Magway, Mandalay), found by LISA and Gi\* and mostly surviving FDR, plus smaller, less certain peripheral ones that mostly fail FDR (@sec-lmsa-robust), Hlaingbwe excepted. EHSA adds support: Dawei and Palaw have been hot every quarter since 2022.
- **Cold spots.** The Wa and eastern Shan hills (most certain), the delta, Yangon and Nay Pyi Taw (least certain: 8 of 23 Low-Low survive FDR).
- **Outliers.** No High-Low outliers: heavy fighting never stands alone. The four Low-High outliers (Pyinoolwin, Myeik, Hlaingbwe, Tonzang) **are all EHSA hot spots in some quarters**, Pyinoolwin only from mid-2024. A Low-High outlier in the total may be a township fighting has not yet reached, or reached briefly; with four cases, a hypothesis, not a finding.

**O2: where, how fast, and in what pattern is violence evolving?**

- **The Dry Zone core persisted.** Eleven townships have been hot every quarter since Q3 or Q4 2021, "consecutive" rather than "persistent" only because they were not significant in early 2021.
- **It spread at a measurable pace.** Madaya (Q4 2022), Mogoke (Q4 2023), Pyinoolwin (Q3 2024), Nyaung-U and Chauk (Q1 2025): about one township every two to three quarters, north-east and south along the Ayeyarwady.
- **Other fronts were short.** Northern Shan was hot for two quarters (Q4 2023, Q1 2024) and cold by 2025. Rakhine went cold (2021–2023), hot (2024), then quiet except Kyaukpyu. Kayah and Chin were hot in 2021–2023 and have faded.
- **Where the war is now.** In Q3 2025, `r sum(sig_hot[, ncol(sig_hot)])` townships are significant hot spots and `r sum(sig_cold[, ncol(sig_cold)])` cold spots.

**Air and ground.** Airstrikes follow the rest of the war (@sec-bivariate): the 29 High-High townships hold a third of all strikes, 43 of the 47 Low-Low townships have none, and no township has many strikes among quiet neighbours.

## How much to trust each finding

| Finding | Evidence | Strength | Main weakness |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Dry Zone core is a hot spot | LISA High-High, Gi\* 99%, EHSA consecutive, hot in all six runs; 17 of 28 High-High survive FDR | **Strong** | Class label sits on the 90% boundary |
| Wa and Shan hills are cold spots | LISA Low-Low, Gi\* 99%, EHSA persistent; 18 of 21 survive FDR | **Strong** | Zero events may reflect access and reporting, not peace (@sec-limitations) |
| Delta and Yangon are cold spots | LISA Low-Low, EHSA persistent or consecutive cold | **Moderate** | Only 8 of 23 survive FDR |
| Northern Shan was a short hot spot | EHSA timeline, two significant quarters; absent from the total | **Moderate** | Class label changes with the threshold |
| Rakhine went cold, hot, then quiet | EHSA timeline; matches independent sources | **Moderate** | Labelled "no pattern" because no category covers it |
| Tanintharyi and Kayin are hot spots | EHSA: 13–16 hot quarters | **Moderate** | Fail FDR in the whole-period analysis |
| Low-High outliers | Four in LISA, five in the bivariate analysis | **Weak** | One survives FDR; the bivariate set is unstable |
| Airstrikes follow the ground war | Bivariate I = 0.44; clusters stable in every variant | **Strong** for clusters, **weak** for outliers | Strikes include resistance drones |

: Strength of evidence for the main findings

The exact EHSA class is the least reliable output (78% keep it at threshold 0.025, 67% on the monthly cube; @sec-ehsa-sens). Family and timeline are far more stable, so classes are read as shorthand for the timelines.

# Peace-keeping implications {#sec-peacekeeping}

The brief hopes the results can help peace-building. Three kinds of statement are kept apart: **Evidence** (what this analysis shows), **Inference** (what it reasonably suggests) and **Beyond the data** (outside context or speculation the statistics cannot confirm). Counts show where violence was *reported*, not harm to people, and nothing here is a forecast.

## Plan for lasting hot spots, not only for surges

**Evidence.** Eleven Dry Zone townships have been hot every quarter since the second half of 2021. The `r sum(integ$n_hot6 == 6)` townships hot in all six EHSA runs hold `r scales::percent(sum(integ$conflict_n[integ$n_hot6 == 6]) / sum(integ$conflict_n), accuracy = 1)` of reported events and `r round(sum(integ$pop2014[integ$n_hot6 == 6], na.rm = TRUE) / 1e6, 1)` million of the analysed townships' 47.6 million people (2014 census).

**Inference.** In the Dry Zone core, conflict is a standing condition, not a spike. Civilian protection, humanitarian access and service continuity need a long-term posture, with @fig-map-integrated as a baseline township list.

**Beyond the data.** The 2014 census is old and incomplete. OCHA reported 3.6 million internally displaced and 19.9 million in need in 2025, with the response plan 12% funded in mid-August [@ocha2025]. Overlaying displacement and access data is the obvious next step, not done here.

## Watch the edges of emerging fronts

**Evidence.** Hot spots spread at about one new township every two to three quarters (@sec-ehsa-results). All four whole-period Low-High outliers are EHSA hot spots at some time; Pyinoolwin became one in 2024.

```{r}
#| label: watchlist
# Townships whose first significant hot quarter is Q1 2024 or later, and that were hot in at least
# three of the last four quarters
first_hot_idx <- apply(sig_hot, 1, \(r) if (any(r)) which(r)[1] else NA)
last4_hot     <- rowSums(sig_hot[, (ncol(sig_hot) - 3):ncol(sig_hot)])

ehsa |>
  mutate(first_hot_idx = first_hot_idx, hot_last4 = last4_hot) |>
  filter(first_hot_idx >= 13, hot_last4 >= 3) |>
  arrange(first_hot_idx) |>
  transmute(State = ST, Township = TS, `EHSA class` = class, `First hot quarter` = first_hot,
            `Hot quarters` = hot_q, `Events, 2021–25` = conflict_n,
            `Trend p-value` = signif(mk_p, 2)) |>
  kable()
```

**Inference.** The table lists townships that turned hot recently and are still rising. Three (Pyinoolwin, Chauk, Nyaung-U) have under 130 events in total, so a map of totals would miss them. A watch-list based on rising quarterly Gi\* would warn earlier, starting with townships next to the active front, such as those around Pyinoolwin.

**Beyond the data.** Why fighting moves into a township (a military operation, a resistance offensive, a collapsing local ceasefire) cannot be read from counts. The Mandalay-side spread matches reporting on Operation 1027's second phase [@iiss2024mandalay]; we found no source for the 2025 spread along the Ayeyarwady.

## Treat quiet townships as unknown, not safe

**Evidence.** Cold spots cover the Wa and eastern Shan hills (the Wa townships report no events at all), the delta, Yangon and Nay Pyi Taw. Rakhine is mostly "no pattern" in 2025 after a hot 2024. Yangon fell clearly from 240–330 events a quarter in 2021 to 40–80 from 2023.

**Inference.** A cold spot means fewer events were *recorded* than chance would give. In the Wa hills that fits the long-standing ceasefire; in Yangon, armed conflict moved away.

**Beyond the data.** Quiet does not mean safe. Reporting depends on access, and the data cannot separate no fighting from unreported fighting, so quiet townships need other sources before any conclusion.

## Ceasefires need verification

**Evidence.** After the 28 March 2025 earthquake, the military, the National Unity Government and several ethnic armed groups announced unilateral ceasefires. The table compares daily event rates.

```{r}
#| label: ceasefire-check
quake <- conflict_ts |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(air = sub_event_type == "Air/drone strike")

tribble(~period,                                    ~start,       ~end,
        "Before (1 Jan – 27 Mar 2025)",             "2025-01-01", "2025-03-27",
        "Earthquake ceasefires (28 Mar – 18 Apr)",  "2025-03-28", "2025-04-18",
        "After (19 Apr – 30 Jun 2025)",             "2025-04-19", "2025-06-30") |>
  mutate(across(c(start, end), as.Date), days = as.numeric(end - start) + 1) |>
  pmap_dfr(\(period, start, end, days) {
    x <- filter(quake, event_date >= start, event_date <= end)
    tibble(period, days,
           events_per_day = round(nrow(x) / days, 1),
           air_drone_strikes_per_day = round(sum(x$air) / days, 1))
  }) |>
  kable()
```

Armed-conflict events fell by about a fifth in the ceasefire window, but air and drone strikes did not fall at all, consistent with ACLED's count of 211 military airstrikes between 28 March and 18 April [@acled_quake]. In the north, Operation 1027's two hot quarters ended around the January 2024 China-brokered ceasefire (@sec-ehsa-results).

**Inference.** The timing fits brokered ceasefires lowering *ground* fighting where observed while air attacks continued. Of the seven northern Shan townships hot in Q4 2023 and Q1 2024, none was hot again, and four (Laukkaing, Kunlong, Hopang, Kutkai) were significant cold spots by mid-2025.

**Beyond the data.** The data cannot show that ceasefires *caused* these changes rather than displacing violence, and the earthquake may itself have reduced reporting. ACLED notes no mechanism was set up to monitor the earthquake ceasefires or coordinate relief [@acled_quake]. After the window, the TNLA agreed a China-brokered ceasefire on 29 October 2025 and handed Mogoke, a Dry Zone spread hot spot here, to the military [@dvb2025mogok]. Monitored ceasefires, checked against event data like these, would be more credible than declarations.

## Air power follows the ground war, so civilians in hot spots face both

**Evidence.** Airstrikes concentrate in the same Dry Zone townships as other fighting: the High-High townships hold a third of all strikes (@sec-bivariate), and no township has many strikes among quiet neighbours. About 71% of strikes have state forces as first actor; most others are by resistance forces.

**Inference.** There is no sign of air power aimed at areas without other fighting. Civilians in the core hot spots face both ground and aerial violence, and risk-reduction measures (shelter, strike early warning, medical access) should assume both.

**Beyond the data.** ACLED reports 1,134 military airstrikes in January–May 2025 against 640 a year earlier, and at least 158 civilians killed by military drone strikes [@acled2025drones]. Strike counts do not show who was hit, nor whether the five Low-High townships reflect different military priorities.

# Limitations {#sec-limitations}

**Data.**

- **Events are reported events.** ACLED relies on media, local reports and partners. Where access is poor, as in the Wa townships (no events) or Rakhine during blockades and shutdowns, counts understate conflict, so cold spots mean "fewer events recorded", not "less violence".
- **Counts are not harm.** A skirmish and a massacre count once each; fatalities are secondary because they are less certain (@sec-fatalities).
- **Location is approximate.** Precision-3 events were dropped and 180 events reassigned across a shared boundary (@sec-reconcile); some events near boundaries may still be misplaced.
- **Counts are not rates** (D1). The only populations are from the 2014 census, old and incomplete, so a small township with many events looks like a large one with the same count.
- **The window is fixed** at 30 September 2025. EHSA weights the final quarter (Monywa is "sporadic" because it was not significant in Q3 2025), so later events could change several classes. Post-window ceasefires and handovers (@sec-peacekeeping) are outside the analysis.
- **The airstrike variable mixes actors.** State forces are first actor in about 71% of strikes (@sec-bivariate).

**Method.**

- **The unit shapes the result.** Townships range from Yangon wards of a few km² to Kachin and Shan townships of thousands; another scale or boundary set could show a different pattern (MAUP; @openshaw1984).
- **Gi\* is relative.** Each quarter is standardised on itself, so a township can lose hot status because fighting grew elsewhere, as Chin did (@sec-ehsa-results).
- **Neighbours are shared boundaries**, regardless of terrain, roads or front lines. KNN runs show the conclusions change only at the margins (@sec-lmsa-robust, @sec-ehsa-sens).
- **Edge effects.** Border and coastal townships have fewer neighbours and noisier statistics.
- **Multiple testing.** 329 township tests (and 6,251 township-quarter tests in EHSA) run at a nominal 5%. About half of the LISA and Gi\* results survive FDR; EHSA classes are not corrected, as the rules depend on counts of significant quarters.
- **EHSA labels are fragile.** Only 78% keep their class at 0.025 and 67% on the monthly cube, and the 90% rule puts the Dry Zone core just below "persistent". Family and timeline are more stable (@sec-ehsa-sens). Successive quarters are likely correlated, so Mann–Kendall p-values are probably too optimistic.
- **A modified EHSA implementation.** `sfdep` was not used as is (position matching, pooled permutations, one mis-signed rule). The replacement reproduces its Gi\* to rounding error (@sec-ehsa-impl) but is a departure from the standard tool.
- **Bivariate LISA is asymmetric and descriptive.** It shows co-location, not influence. Its Low-High outliers are unstable (one survives FDR), and results depend on which variable sits in the township.
- **No causal claims.** Outside context is marked as such; matching dates are consistent with a link but do not show one.

# Design decisions {#sec-geovis}

<details>
<summary>Click to expand: the reasoning behind each map's design</summary>

This section records the design choices behind those maps, including the alternative forms considered, the colour logic, and how the figures work together, for anyone who wants the reasoning rather than the results.

## Choices for each visual

| Visual | Question it answers | Form chosen | Alternatives rejected, and why |
|----|----|----|----|
| Count map (@fig-map-counts) | Where do events pile up? | Choropleth, five Fisher–Jenks classes, zero as its own class | Equal and quantile breaks: one colour, or hidden extremes (@sec-lmsa). Density: dominated by tiny Yangon wards (@sec-assumptions) |
| LISA and Gi\* maps (@fig-map-lisa, @fig-map-gistar) | Which townships are significant? | Only p \< 0.05 coloured, the rest grey, as the brief requires | All values: invites reading non-significant townships |
| Robustness map (@fig-map-robust) | How many specifications agree? | Count of runs in which a township is hot or cold | One map per specification: four near-identical maps hide the differences |
| EHSA class map (@fig-map-ehsa) | What is each township's final pattern? | Eight observed classes, hot to cold | All 17 classes: nine never occur |
| EHSA timeline (@fig-ehsa-timeline) | How did that pattern arise? | Township × quarter tile grid, grouped by front | 19 small multiples: the eye cannot follow one township through 19 panels |
| Permutation diagnostic (@fig-ehsa-perm) | Why not use `sfdep` as is? | Three aligned time series | A table: the problem is a *trend* across quarters |
| Bivariate LISA map (@fig-map-bivariate) | Do airstrikes follow other fighting? | Same four-class design as @fig-map-lisa, for comparison | A bivariate choropleth: shows values, not significance |
| Interactive EHSA map (@fig-ehsa-interactive) | Which township is which, and what is its history? | Same classes and colours as @fig-map-ehsa, with names on hover and details on click | Labels on the static map: 329 names are unreadable at page size |
| Evidence map (@fig-map-integrated) | Where do the methods agree? | Five classes, dark for "total and time", light for "time only" | A table alone: hides the geography |

: Visual design decisions

## Colour, legends and map furniture

- **Sequential colour for counts, diverging for statistics.** Counts run yellow to dark red; hot and cold spots use red and blue around a grey "not significant", because the question is the *sign* of the departure. Red–blue stays distinguishable for most colour-blind readers, and classes also differ in lightness.
- **Colours keep one meaning.** Red is more conflict than expected, blue less; dark is more certain or persistent.
- **EHSA colours follow the classification.** Hot: dark red (consecutive), orange (oscillating), pale salmon (sporadic). Cold: dark blue (persistent), mid blue (consecutive), teal (oscillating), pale blue (sporadic).
- **Map furniture is kept light.** Each static map carries a north arrow and a scale bar (0–100–200 km), placed in empty corners, so distances can be read. Township labels are left off, because 329 names are unreadable at this size; the text states the data source, state and region outlines orient the reader, and the interactive map (@fig-ehsa-interactive) carries the names.
- **Legends sit outside the map panel**, to the right, so they never cover townships, and their titles state the p-value threshold where relevant.
- **Captions say what is hidden.** Every significance map notes that only p \< 0.05 townships are coloured and Cocokyun is excluded.
- **Commentary stays within the brief's 200 words per visual** and starts with the statistic before outside context. Each findings figure also has a plain-language paragraph beneath it.

## Narrative flow

The visuals form one argument. The count map (@fig-map-counts) shows *that* conflict is uneven; the LISA and Gi\* maps test whether that beats chance, and the robustness map how far the answer depends on choices. The EHSA maps and timeline add time, the bivariate map relates two kinds of violence, and the evidence map combines them. A shared base map, state outlines and red-to-blue logic mean readers learn the design once.

</details>

# Reproducibility {#sec-reproducibility}

<details>
<summary>Click to expand: data, code and software needed to reproduce this analysis</summary>

This section lists what another analyst needs to re-run the report and get the same results: the data, the folder layout, the steps to render, how randomness is controlled, and the software versions used.

## Data and folder layout

The report expects the following structure inside the Quarto project. Paths in the code are relative to the folder that holds this file, so the project can be moved without editing the code.

```
Take-home_Ex02/
├── Take-home_Ex02_TH.qmd
├── Take-home_Ex02_ES.qmd
├── references.bib
├── images/
└── data/
    ├── aspatial/
    │   └── ACLED_Data_Myanmar_Jan2021-Sep2025.csv
    ├── geospatial/
    │   └── myanmar_township_boundaries.*   (MIMU v9.4 shapefile)
    └── rds/                                (written by the report)
```

**Data availability.** ACLED's terms of use restrict redistribution of its event data, so the raw extract is not included in the GitHub repository. It is available to course participants on eLearn, or can be requested from ACLED for Myanmar, 1 January 2021 to 30 September 2025. Save it as `data/aspatial/ACLED_Data_Myanmar_Jan2021-Sep2025.csv`. The MIMU v9.4 township boundaries are publicly available from the MIMU GeoNode [@mimu_township]; save all shapefile components with the layer name `myanmar_township_boundaries` in `data/geospatial/`.

## Running the analysis

1. Install R and the packages listed below. `pacman::p_load()` at the start of data preparation installs any that are missing.
2. Place the two data sets as shown above.
3. Render `Take-home_Ex02_TH.qmd`. The report runs top to bottom without manual steps. Intermediate results are saved to `data/rds/` as they are produced, so later sections reload the same objects rather than recomputing them.
4. Render `Take-home_Ex02_ES.qmd` after the report. The deck reads every number and map from `data/rds/deck_objects.rds`, written by the report's final appendix, so the two documents cannot disagree.

The report uses `freeze: auto`, so Quarto reuses saved results until the source changes. Delete the `_freeze/` folder to force a complete re-run.

## Controlling randomness

Every permutation test (Moran's I, LISA, Gi\*, bivariate LISA and the EHSA permutations) runs 999 simulations after `set.seed(2025)`. Sensitivity runs that test the effect of the seed use `set.seed(2026)` and say so. With the same data, seeds and package versions, every p-value, class and count in this report is reproduced exactly.

## Software environment

```{r}
#| label: package-versions
pkgs <- c("sf", "spdep", "sfdep", "lwgeom", "tmap", "classInt",
          "Kendall", "tidyverse", "knitr")

tibble(Package = pkgs,
       Version = map_chr(pkgs, \(p) as.character(packageVersion(p)))) |>
  bind_rows(tibble(Package = "R",
                   Version = paste(R.version$major, R.version$minor, sep = "."))) |>
  kable(caption = "R and package versions used to render this report")
```

The full session information below also lists the operating system and every package loaded indirectly, such as `s2` and `units` under `sf`.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Full session information

```{r}
#| label: session-info
sessionInfo()
```
:::

</details>

# Use of AI {#sec-ai}

Following the completion of independent analysis, generative AI tools were employed exclusively to enhance the linguistic clarity and readability of the technical report. My original methodology, analytical insights, code, and conclusions remain completely unassisted.

During the development process in R Studio, generative AI was utilized for auxiliary tasks such as discovering layout features, adding images, and implementing workflows. It was also used to quickly summarize libraries, with official documentation consulted directly whenever a deeper dive was required.

# Appendix: objects for the Executive Summary {.appendix}

The Executive Summary deck reads the results below from one file, so its numbers always match this report.

```{r}
#| label: save-deck-objects
air <- conflict_ts |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(sub_event_type == "Air/drone strike")

deck_objects <- list(
  funnel        = funnel,
  mmr_conflict  = mmr_conflict |> select(TS_PCODE, ST, TS, conflict_n, airstrike_n, pop2014),
  mmr_states    = mmr_states,
  count_breaks  = count_breaks,
  count_labels  = count_labels,
  global_moran  = unname(gm[[1]]$statistic),
  lisa          = lisa |> select(TS_PCODE, ST, TS, conflict_n, lisa_class, p_fdr),
  hcsa          = hcsa |> select(TS_PCODE, ST, TS, hcsa_class, p_fdr),
  robust        = robust |> select(TS_PCODE, ST, TS, n_hot, n_cold, robustness),
  bv            = bv |> select(TS_PCODE, ST, TS, bv_class, airstrike_n, other_n, p_bh),
  bv_I          = bv_global$t0,
  bv_p          = (sum(bv_global$t >= bv_global$t0) + 1) / (length(bv_global$t) + 1),
  ehsa          = ehsa |> select(TS_PCODE, ST, TS, conflict_n, class, family, hot_q, cold_q,
                                 first_hot, tau, mk_p),
  ehsa_pal      = ehsa_pal,
  ehsa_levels   = ehsa_levels,
  ehsa_n_hot6   = sum(ehsa_sens$n_hot == 6),
  ehsa_n_cold6  = sum(ehsa_sens$n_cold == 6),
  ehsa_class_kept = c(thr_025 = mean(ehsa_sens$thr_025 == ehsa_sens$primary),
                      monthly = mean(ehsa_sens$monthly == ehsa_sens$primary)),
  timeline      = timeline,
  q_labels      = q_labels,
  integ         = integ |> select(TS_PCODE, ST, TS, conflict_n, gi, evidence,
                                  n_hot6, n_cold6, pop2014),
  watch         = ehsa |>
                    mutate(first_hot_idx = first_hot_idx, hot_last4 = last4_hot) |>
                    filter(first_hot_idx >= 13, hot_last4 >= 3) |>
                    arrange(first_hot_idx) |>
                    select(ST, TS, class, first_hot, hot_q, conflict_n),
  quake         = tribble(~period, ~start, ~end,
                          "Before",                "2025-01-01", "2025-03-27",
                          "Earthquake ceasefires", "2025-03-28", "2025-04-18",
                          "After",                 "2025-04-19", "2025-06-30") |>
                    mutate(across(c(start, end), as.Date), days = as.numeric(end - start) + 1) |>
                    pmap_dfr(\(period, start, end, days) {
                      x <- filter(quake, event_date >= start, event_date <= end)
                      tibble(period, events_per_day = round(nrow(x) / days, 1),
                             air_per_day = round(sum(x$air) / days, 1))
                    }),
  n_air         = nrow(air),
  air_state     = mean(air$inter1 == "State forces")
)

write_rds(deck_objects, "data/rds/deck_objects.rds")
```
